title: The Pentecost novena
hookLine: the first novena, from Ascension to Pentecost

cards: The friends of Jesus are walking back into Jerusalem from the hill called Olivet. A short walk. He's gone from their sight, in a way none of them can explain, and before he went he told them to wait.
Not to preach yet, not to organize, not to scatter. Wait. So they climb the stairs to an upper room and do the one thing they've been asked to do.
Nobody tells them how long it will take.

teach.b: Acts lists who's in the room, name by name: Peter and John, James and Andrew, and the rest.
Then it adds more, in the Douay-Rheims: "All these were persevering with one mind in prayer with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brethren."
So what tradition calls the first novena was not one person alone with a leaflet. It was a room full of people: women, unnamed here, Jesus's family, his mother.
Persevering, with one mind, in prayer, they wait for something they've been promised and can't produce themselves. Then the end of the waiting.
Acts two opens, in the Douay-Rheims: "And when the days of the Pentecost were accomplished, they were all together in one place."

Pentecost was already a Jewish feast, the harvest feast Jews still keep as Shavuot, which is why the city is crowded with pilgrims. Then comes a sound from heaven like a mighty wind, tongues like fire, and the Spirit.
Notice where it finds them: all together. Tradition counts the days from the Ascension to Pentecost as nine, and keeps them as a novena to the Holy Spirit.
Pope Leo the Thirteenth, in a letter on the Holy Spirit, asked the whole Church to make that novena every year, and some parishes still mark it.
One prayer used is just three words: Come, Holy Spirit.

teach.h: PERSEVERING WITH ONE MIND IN PRAYER.
teach.b: They open an old hymn and a well-worn prayer, and they say exactly what the upper room was doing. Waiting together is different from waiting alone. Someone else keeps the vigil when you nod off.

how: Between the Ascension and Pentecost, some Catholics and parishes pray a novena to the Holy Spirit, often using the words come, Holy Spirit, or the hymns that begin with them.

o: the prayers said on Pentecost day itself
nine days of prayer to the Spirit before Pentecost
a nine-day fast kept before Christmas each year

games.q: the Pentecost novena — tap the pairs.

s: Acts says the apostles prayed for exactly nine days
Acts doesn't count them. tradition counts the days from the Ascension to Pentecost as nine.
Mary was in the upper room with the apostles
Acts names her: Mary the mother of Jesus, with the women and his brethren.
Pentecost began as a Christian feast
it was already a Jewish feast, which Jews keep as Shavuot.

games.q: you're one of the friends of Jesus, back from Olivet. he's gone from sight, and he told you to wait. what do you do?
o: go home and get on with life.
gather with the others and pray.
start preaching in the streets right away.
games.why: they go up to the upper room and persevere with one mind in prayer, together, until the Spirit comes at Pentecost.

practice: Bring to mind the people you're waiting alongside right now: a family waiting on news, coworkers waiting on a decision, a friend waiting to heal.

If you pray, say the three words slowly on the out-breath, Come, Holy Spirit, and let them go out for the whole room, not only for yourself. If you don't pray, simply breathe out for those people, one by one.

wordCard.voice: The Pentecost novena. The days between the Ascension and Pentecost, kept as nine days of prayer to the Holy Spirit, in the pattern of the upper room.

carryVoice: Your line: waiting together. The Spirit found them all in one place. Rest well.
